text: Ruth Mildred Barker (February 3, 1897 – January 25, 1990) was a musician, scholar, manager, and spiritual leader from the Alfred and Sabbathday Lake Shaker villages. Born in Providence, Rhode Island on February 3, 1897, she joined the Shakers on July 7, 1903, when her newly widowed mother placed her under the care of the Alfred village. She was assigned to the Second Family, where sister Harriet Coolbroth served as a mother figure, and she assisted the elderly sister Paulina Springer, with whom she befriended and learned the song "Mother Has Come with Her Beautiful Song." Springer died in 1905 and, on her deathbed, asked Barker to always remain Shaker, a promise Barker kept. Barker's interest in music grew through lessons from Coolbroth and Lucinda Taylor, and she later stated that the "vim and vigor" of Shaker song drew her to the faith. She was a member of the "Beacon Light Circle." Her mother returned in 1911 to take her home, but Barker insisted on staying at Alfred, and seven years later, in 1920, she signed the covenant as a member of the Alfred community. The Second Family closed that same year, and Barker moved to the Church Family at Alfred. In 1931, the Alfred community closed, and she relocated to Sabbathday Lake in New Gloucester, Maine, where she was placed in charge of the Girls' Order and formed the "Girls' Improvement Club" for poetry, recitations, and Bible study. She also managed preserves and candy making—specializing in hand-dipped chocolates—at the village store, where she sewed and knitted, overseeing these operations until 1968. In 1950, she was appointed trustee of Sabbathday Lake, responsible for the village’s businesses and finances. Since the 1940s, she served as de facto spiritual leader of the Sabbathday Lake community. Gertrude Soule, who had left and rejoined the community multiple times, was appointed Eldress in 1950 and felt uncomfortable with Barker’s influence. In 1957, Soule moved to the Parent Ministry at Hancock Shaker Village in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. In 1971, after Soule decided not to return to Sabbathday Lake, Barker was appointed Eldress in her place. In 1960, Theodore Johnson joined the Shakers, and the following year, he and Barker co-founded The Shaker Quarterly, a magazine and journal that published scholarly articles on theology and the Shakers, shared village news, and occasionally advertised community products. Barker served as business manager from its founding until 1974 and regularly contributed articles and the newsletter column Home Notes. Through her leadership, Sabbathday Lake reopened its religious meetings to public attendance. She traveled as a speaker on Shaker-related topics. From the 1940s onward, she worked with historian and musicologist Daniel W. Patterson to preserve Shaker music. She noted that she initially did not realize how vital the music was, but felt a deep connection to the tradition, believing it was essential and would endure through centuries. She appeared on four recordings, including Early Shaker Spirituals. In recognition of her contributions to traditional Shaker song, she received the National Heritage Fellowship in 1983 from the National Endowment for the Arts. She also received numerous other awards. Barker died on January 25, 1990, after battling cancer for several months.
